explanation: byte range is -128 to 127; 128 overflows to -128 in two's complement representation.
f and d have different precision; 0.1 cannot be exactly represented in binary floating-point, causing inequality after type conversion.
Cast truncates the long to int range (-2^31 to 2^31-1); 5000000000 exceeds this and wraps to a negative value.
char 'A' is ASCII 65; adding 1 gives 66, casting to char gives 'B'.
b1 && (b2 = true) uses short-circuit AND; b1 is true so it evaluates the right side, assigning b2 to true, returning true; second print shows b2 is now true.
Integer.toString creates a new String object, so reference equality (==) is false; content equality (.equals) would be true.
1.0 / 0.0 returns Positive Infinity (IEEE 754 standard), and it equals Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY.
x++ returns the original value (5) then increments x to 6, so y=5 and x=6.
new Integer() creates distinct objects (a == b is false), but 10 is in the integer cache (-128 to 127), so c and d reference the same object (c == d is true).
String concatenation calls toString() on the null reference, which produces the string 'null', then appends 'x' to get 'nullx'.
